name: Trump's Wall
seoTitle: Trump's Wall Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Trump's Wall: work out total panel volume from the length and the height. A free construction calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Trump's Wall calculator the length, the height, the panel length and the panel width and it returns total panel volume. It is built for a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Trump's Wall calculator work?
sections.html:
The Trump's Wall calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports total panel volume in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the length, the height, the panel length and the panel width.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Trump's Wall calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Total panel volume=((1 ÷ 1250) × panel length × (1250 × foundation length × foundation width + 1250 × height × panel width + 1143 × panel width))
Number of panels=(length ÷ panel length)
Total concrete=((length ÷ panel length) × ((1 ÷ 1250) × panel length × (1250 × foundation length × foundation width + 1250 × height × panel width + 1143 × panel width)))
Manufacturing cost=(price of pre-cast, reinforced concrete × ((length ÷ panel length) × ((1 ÷ 1250) × panel length × (1250 × foundation length × foundation width + 1250 × height × panel width + 1143 × panel width))))
Assembly cost per element=((1 ÷ 60) × assembly time per element × (bulldozer operator's wage + bulldozer rent + construction worker's wage × construction workers needed + crane operator's wage + crane rent + excavator operator's wage + excavator rent) ÷ assembly time efficiency)
Total assembly cost=((length ÷ panel length) × ((1 ÷ 60) × assembly time per element × (bulldozer operator's wage + bulldozer rent + construction worker's wage × construction workers needed + crane operator's wage + crane rent + excavator operator's wage + excavator rent) ÷ assembly time efficiency))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Trump's Wall calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the length, the height and the panel length — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Trump's Wall calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns total panel volume, derived from the length, the height and the panel length. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Trump's Wall calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the length, the height, the panel length and the panel width, which is 26 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter length in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Length opens in miles and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Total project cost = 8379421866632820. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Trump's Wall calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
